title: Nvidia and AMD Lobby Trump to Kill New China Chip Curbs, as Beijing Weighs Letting ByteDance and Alibaba Buy Nvidia Again
subhead: US chipmakers are pushing back hard against a defense bill that would cut China off from AI processors, while Beijing signals it may reopen the door to Nvidia sales for its biggest tech firms. Meanwhile SpaceX's Starship reached orbit for the first time.

sections.heading: Chipmakers Fight the Defense Bill
sections.body:
Nvidia and AMD are lobbying the Trump administration to intervene against new China-related chip export restrictions being written into a defense bill, according to Politico, Reuters and Benzinga. Politico framed the standoff plainly: lawmakers plan to cut China off from AI chips, and the two chipmakers want the White House to step in. The lobbying push is notable because it comes just days after the Trump-Xi summit in Washington produced no breakthrough on semiconductor policy.

The defense bill avenue matters because it is harder for the executive branch to quietly soften than an agency rule. If Congress writes strict China chip language into must-pass legislation, chipmakers lose the flexibility they have used in past rounds of controls.
sections.whyItMatters: The fight has shifted from whether to restrict China to who gets to decide — and chipmakers are betting the White House will shield them from Congress. That is a new front in the export-control battle.

sections.heading: Beijing Signals It May Let ByteDance and Alibaba Buy Nvidia Chips
sections.body:
In a parallel move, China is weighing allowing ByteDance and Alibaba to buy new Nvidia chips, specifically the RTX Pro 5500, according to reporting by The Information carried by Reuters, Bloomberg, Quartz and Seeking Alpha. The deliberations, reported over the past three days, reportedly reflect a shortfall in domestic alternatives — Seoul Economic Daily cast it as China weighing approval 'as Huawei falls short.'

The scale involved is large: Barchart reported ByteDance could theoretically buy up to 1 million Nvidia GPUs, though it cautioned the figure is speculative. Any approval would be partial and political, not a return to open trade — the RTX Pro 5500 is a workstation-class part, not Nvidia's top training silicon.
sections.whyItMatters: Two opposing pressures are now visible at once: Washington tightening the screws in legislation, Beijing selectively loosening its own import stance to keep its AI labs fed. China's domestic chip push is not yet covering the gap at the high end.

sections.heading: Starship Reaches Orbit for the First Time, Deploys 26 V3 Starlinks
sections.body:
SpaceX's Starship reached orbit for the first time on Flight 14, deploying 26 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites before the mission ended early, according to Reuters, Ars Technica, Space and SpaceX. Ars Technica described it as SpaceX's orbital debut for the vehicle; The Register noted engine trouble cut the victory lap short. Elon Musk said the flight was a success and that Starship is targeting a weekly launch cadence in 2027, per BASENOR and 24/7 Wall St.

The V3 satellites are the heavier, higher-capacity generation that Starship — not Falcon 9 — was designed to carry. Reaching orbit with a live payload, even a truncated mission, moves Starlink's next build-out from paper to demonstrated capability.
sections.whyItMatters: Orbital Starship with real payloads is the precondition for scaling Starlink to its next generation. A weekly cadence target, if met, would change the economics of orbital bandwidth and launch capacity.

sections.heading: Brussels Moves to Give Telcos More Time on Huawei and ZTE
sections.body:
European governments and telecom operators may get more time to phase out high-risk Chinese equipment under a new EU proposal, Reuters reported, with EU Today framing it as governments seeking more time to remove high-risk Chinese telecom gear. The proposal would extend the phase-out timetable covering vendors such as Huawei and ZTE.

Separately, Cambodia's CellCard lined up a roughly $300 million network overhaul led by Huawei, per Developing Telecoms and Telecompaper — a reminder that in much of the world Huawei's 5G footprint is expanding, not contracting.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe is slowing the removal of Chinese gear even as it says the risk is real — a sign that cost and 5G deployment timelines are winning out over security deadlines. The Huawei phase-out is becoming a schedule problem, not a settled policy.

sections.heading: China Widens Travel Curbs to Families of Top AI and Chip Talent
sections.body:
Beijing has broadened overseas travel restrictions to cover the families of senior AI and semiconductor talent, according to Bloomberg (via The Japan Times, The Standard and Seoul Economic Daily). The measure extends controls that previously applied to the engineers and executives themselves to their relatives.

The move is a talent-retention tool aimed at stopping elite researchers leaving for US firms or competitors. WION called it an 'AI talent firewall.' It sits alongside reports in Korea JoongAng Daily alleging CXMT ran a campaign of blackmail, poaching and theft to obtain Samsung memory technology, including testimony from a former Samsung manager.
sections.whyItMatters: China is treating top AI and chip engineers as strategic assets to be locked in place. That both reflects the value of the talent pool and hints at concern about how much of it would leave if allowed.

sections.heading: Samsung Puts $1B Into Nvidia-Backed AI Infrastructure Firm Helix
sections.body:
Samsung will invest $1 billion in AI infrastructure company Helix, an Nvidia-backed firm, according to Samsung's newsroom and Analytics India Magazine. The deal ties a major memory and foundry player directly into the AI data-center build-out — Samsung supplies the high-bandwidth memory that AI accelerators depend on.

In India, the compute conversation is shifting from raw GPU counts to utilization. ET Datacenters and dqindia.com both reported that India's AI compute strategy needs to focus on turning compute into value, not just buying GPUs, while CRN Asia reported IBM partnering with Yotta to build a sovereign AI stack for Indian enterprises.
sections.whyItMatters: Memory and infrastructure — not just logic chips — are becoming the contested layer. Samsung's bet and India's 'value over GPUs' debate both point to the same bottleneck: what you do with compute matters as much as owning it.

sections.heading: Türkiye Angle: South Korea Eyes Turkish Drone Engines
sections.body:
South Korea has asked Türkiye about buying TEI's PD170 drone engine, according to Türkiye Today, The Defence Blog and Korean outlet JKN. JKN reported the interest follows a string of crashes in South Korea's domestic drone programs, pushing Seoul to look at proven Turkish engines.

It is a notable reversal of the usual direction of technology transfer — a major Asian manufacturing economy evaluating a Turkish defense-tech supplier for a critical component. Teknofest is also set to bring technology and aviation events to southeastern Türkiye, per Hürriyet Daily News.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkish drone-engine technology is moving from a domestic program to an exportable component that allied militaries are actively shopping for. That is a real, if narrow, win for Türkiye's defense-tech positioning.

bottomLine: Today's story is the collision between policy and the chip market. Nvidia and AMD are lobbying Trump to block a defense bill that would cut China off from AI processors, while Beijing simultaneously weighs letting ByteDance and Alibaba buy Nvidia's RTX Pro 5500 because domestic alternatives fall short. Neither side is converging on a clean decoupling — Washington is tightening in legislation, China is selectively loosening imports, and both are hedging. Elsewhere, Starship's first orbital flight with 26 V3 Starlink payloads moved SpaceX's next-generation constellation from plan to demonstrated capability, and Europe signaled it will give telcos more time to rip out Huawei gear. The pattern for the week: rules are getting harder to write and slower to enforce than either Washington or Beijing would like.
